question: A 25-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and X-rays show a fracture of the proximal ulna with anterior dislocation of the radial head. Which eponymous fracture-dislocation is this, and which nerve is at risk?

answers.text: Galeazzi fracture-dislocation; anterior interosseous nerve at risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Galeazzi fracture involves the distal third of the radius with DRUJ disruption — not the proximal ulna. The mnemonic: Galeazzi = distal radius + DRUJ; Monteggia = proximal ulna + proximal RUJ.

answers.text: Monteggia fracture-dislocation; posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) at risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Monteggia = proximal ulna fracture + radial head dislocation. The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) winds around the radial neck through the radial tunnel and is directly at risk when the radial head dislocates anteriorly. Check for finger/thumb extension deficit.

answers.text: Monteggia fracture-dislocation; anterior interosseous nerve at risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Monteggia is correct, but the nerve at risk is the posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve), not the AIN. AIN injury causes loss of FPL + FDP to index finger (weakness of 'OK sign').
Essex-Lopresti is a radial head fracture with interosseous membrane disruption and DRUJ instability — a different and rare injury. It does not primarily present as a proximal ulna fracture.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is a Monteggia fracture-dislocation (proximal ulna + radial head dislocation). The nerve at risk is the posterior interosseous nerve — test active finger and thumb extension.
Excellent. Monteggia = proximal ulna + proximal RUJ. Galeazzi = distal radius + DRUJ. The posterior interosseous nerve is the nerve to test in Monteggia injuries.
